#### Checkpointing a stateful processor — stack and heap at every step

**What is being answered.** The full checkpoint cycle — steady state, commit, crash, resume — and the one requirement the design does not supply.

Two details are worth watching. `store.durable` is **false**: the local state store is fast and dies with the machine, which is why `commit` exists at all. And `copyOf` makes the checkpoint a snapshot rather than a reference, so the processor can keep working while the upload runs.

Step 4 is the requirement stated as code: `if (atomic == false) { cp.offset = 0 }`. The entries landed and the offset did not, so `torn.total` reaches 68 against 45. This design assumes that commit is atomic; it does not make it so.

The animation steps through the code, holding each line long enough to read the STACK (call frames and their locals) and the HEAP (allocated arrays and objects) as they are AT THAT MOMENT. Expand any step to study it on its own.

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch07-system-memory/ch07-system-memory.svg" alt="Checkpointing a stateful processor — stack and heap at every step, 4 steps showing stack and heap" width="980">

<details>
<summary><b>Step 1 of 4</b> — steady state: one entry per (key, window), updated in place</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch07-system-memory/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: steady state: one entry per (key, window), updated in place" width="980">

After 5 events the local store holds 4 entries totalling 23, and `durable` is **false** — it is on local disk, fast and doomed with the machine. That flag is the distinction the next step exists for.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — the commit writes state and offset to durable storage</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch07-system-memory/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: the commit writes state and offset to durable storage" width="980">

`copyOf` is deliberate: the checkpoint is a SNAPSHOT, not a reference, so the processor can keep mutating its store while the upload proceeds. And the Checkpoint carries `offset` = 4 alongside the entries — the pair, in one durable value.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — resuming from the intact pair reproduces the no-crash run</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch07-system-memory/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: resuming from the intact pair reproduces the no-crash run" width="980">

The loop starts at `cp.offset + 1` = 5 and runs 4 times. `total` ends at 45 across 7 entries — identical to a run that never crashed. 23 loaded plus 22 replayed, and that equation is the design's whole claim.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — a torn commit replays the prefix and over-counts</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch07-system-memory/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: a torn commit replays the prefix and over-counts" width="980">

With `atomic` false the entries landed and the offset did not, so `resume` replays from index 1 and `torn.total` reaches 68 — over by the whole 23 the checkpoint already held. The design REQUIRES this commit to be atomic and does not itself provide that.

</details>
